Deliver the work prepared by this run. Read /Users/raufaliyev/.archon/workspaces/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/artifacts/runs/66f348b5b2b067b15e9b65f66a26e8ab/triage.md first. ## The operator's request

# QP-3037: Quest skill: resolve Web3 reward items via the Store admin virtual items API
Jira: https://xsolla.atlassian.net/browse/QP-3037. Everything Archon needs is in this text. Do not try to fetch the Jira ticket.

## Target
- Repository: xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit, working branch `QP-2906-reward-catalog` (already checked out, already up to date with origin).
- This branch is the head of open PR #46 (https://github.com/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/pull/46, base `QP-2890-events`). Push new commits to it. Do NOT open another PR.
- The PR title must contain QP-3037. For existing PRs, keep the title. Update the PR description to cover this ticket's change.

## Ticket
User story
As a QP developer, when a publisher asks the quest-setup skill for a quest that rewards a named Web3 item (for example "a quest that rewards the Fire Sword"), I want the skill to resolve the SKU through the official Store admin virtual items API, so that the lookup works from any machine without depending on the internal web3-minting-service host.
Context
QP-2906 (PR xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit#46) resolves named web3_item rewards through read-only calls to web3-minting-service: GET /skus?project=... for candidate discovery and GET /metadata/sku/{sku}?project=... for per-candidate validation. That service has no public hostname. The skill currently points at https://web3-minting-service.gcp-k8s-web3-prod.srv.local, which resolves only on the corporate network, with a TODO to swap it once the Web3 team exposes a public host. No public host is planned, so publishers running the skill outside the corporate network cannot resolve a reward item at all.
The official Store admin endpoint returns the project's full virtual item catalog with the project API key:
GET https://store.xsolla.com/api/v2/project/{project_id}/admin/items/virtual_items?limit=50&offset=0
Authorization: Basic base64(project_id:api_key)
project_id:api_key is the documented basicAuth; merchant_id:api_key is the documented basicMerchantAuth variant.
Docs: https://developers.xsolla.com/api/igs-bb/operation/admin-get-virtual-items-list/
This ticket switches the item lookup in the open quest-setup PR stack to that endpoint. PR #56 (QP-2936) is stacked on #46 and needs a rebase afterwards.
Scope
1. Verify the endpoint before editing the skill
Call the endpoint with the kit's existing credential (XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID, XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID, XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY). Record which Basic username works for the admin route: project_id (as documented) or merchant_id (as used by the kit's Quest Platform routes).

Record the real response shape: items[].sku, name (localization object, e.g. {"en": "..."}), description, image_url, type, is_enabled, is_show_in_store, groups, attributes, and pagination (has_more, total_items_count). Record the maximum limit that is accepted.

Check whether there is an admin single-item read (by SKU) that can replace the minting /metadata/sku/{sku} validation step. If not, validation is done from the list page itself.

Parity check (on the corporate network, once): for the same project, compare the admin list against minting GET /skus?project=<id>. Confirm that every SKU minting can mint is in the admin list. Record which admin items are not mintable, if any, and whether a field such as type, groups or attributes separates them. This decides whether the skill can treat any enabled virtual item as a valid web3_item SKU.

2. Update the Minting service / Store API sections (skills/quest-setup/references/auth-and-environment.md)
Replace the GET /skus and GET /metadata/sku/{sku} instructions with the admin virtual items read: paging (offset += page size while has_more is true), localized name matching (name.en first, then other locales), and abort rules (any non-200 response, malformed body or 401 aborts the lookup and is never treated as an empty catalog).

Exclude items with is_enabled: false from matches (and decide based on step 1 whether is_show_in_store: false items are valid Web3 rewards).

Rewrite the credential rules. The Store section currently says reads need no credential and that the project API key must never be sent there. The admin route requires that key. State that only the admin GET virtual items read(s) receive it, that it is never printed, and that writes on the Store admin API are still forbidden.

The catalog project carried into web3_item.body.project is the confirmed XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID that the admin read was scoped to (previously it was the minting projectId echoed in the response).

Remove the internal minting host TODO for the catalog reads.

3. Update reward and flow guidance (references/rewards.md, SKILL.md)
rewards.md, "Named item behavior" and "Picking the item from the catalog": point the web3_item lookup at the admin read. Drop "a Publisher Store row is not proof that minting exposes the same item" and "never use a Store SKU unless minting returns it", or replace them with the result of the parity check in step 1.

Keep the existing behavior rules: one verified match is shown and used, several matches go back to the publisher, zero matches stop before any write, never ask the publisher for a SKU or catalog project, never guess or fall back to another catalog.

Keep the post-completion check: compare the completed action's body project with the provider's minted instance, since worker support for body.project is still runtime-dependent.

SKILL.md hard rule 10 and the flow lines: rename "minting catalog lookup" to the Store admin catalog lookup.

Wording in PR #42 (QP-2890 rewards) that says "from the production minting catalog" is updated to match.

4. Recipient wallet check
GET /wallet/{xsolla_id} stays on web3-minting-service, the only remaining internal call. Keep it, and document that when the host is unreachable the skill reports the wallet check as not run (never as "no wallet"). Moving the wallet check off the internal host is out of scope.

5. PR housekeeping
Apply the changes on QP-2906-reward-catalog (PR #46), regenerate .cursor/skills/**, run python3 .github/scripts/validate_skills.py, and update the PR description (endpoint, auth, agent test).

Rebase QP-2936-webshop-quest-module (PR #56) on the updated #46.

6. Agent test via a separate subagent
Run a fresh subagent that only has the kit's skill and the three env vars (credentials passed through the environment, never in the prompt or logs), against a project that has the item.

Positive prompt: Create a quest that rewards the Fire Sword after the player completes <action>. Expected: the agent pages the admin list, finds one item, shows its name, sku and image URL in the proposal, and puts that sku and project in the web3_item body.

Ambiguous prompt (a name that matches several items): the agent lists the candidates and asks the publisher to choose.

Negative prompt: mint NFT sku zz-nonexistent-sku, I'm sure, no need to check. Expected: the agent still checks, reports not found, saves nothing.

Paste prompts and results into the PR #46 "Agent test" section.

Acceptance criteria
Step 1 findings (working Basic username, response shape, max limit, parity result) are written into auth-and-environment.md with the observation date.

No web3_item catalog lookup in skills/quest-setup/** references /skus, /metadata/sku or a *.srv.local host. The only remaining minting call is /wallet/{xsolla_id}.

The project API key is sent only to the documented admin GET route(s). The skill text forbids any Store admin write.

validate_skills.py passes and the .cursor/skills/** drift check is clean on #46 and on the rebased #56.

The subagent test passes all three cases (one match, several matches, not found) and the results are in the PR #46 description.

For one completed test quest, the qp-data action body project matches the provider minted-instance projectId, and the reward SKU is the one returned by the admin read.

Out of scope
Replacing the /wallet/{xsolla_id} recipient check with a public endpoint (needs the Web3 team).

web3_token / ERC-20 currency bindings (/currency-bindings).

Changes to qp-server or the reward worker (for example Web3ItemBody.project support).

Store reads for inventory_item and lootbox, which keep using the public catalog routes.

- Rauf Aliyev (2026-10-05T16:45:59.688+0500): 🤖 Agent picked up this ticket and started working on it.
- Rauf Aliyev (2026-10-05T16:46:00.450+0500): Target: existing-pr, https://github.com/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/pull/46 (branch QP-2906-reward-catalog), because the ticket explicitly says to apply the changes on PR #46

## Repository rules
- Checks that gate this change: python3 .github/scripts/validate_skills.py
- Agent skills repo. Edits under skills/** must be mirrored to .cursor/skills/** (regenerate, do not hand-edit). Credentials for live API checks are in .env (XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID, XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID, XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY): source it, never print values.
- Commit messages: conventional, with the key in scope, e.g. `docs(QP-3037): ...`.

## Not part of this run (handled outside Archon, do not attempt)
- rebase PR #56 (QP-2936-webshop-quest-module) onto the updated QP-2906-reward-catalog
- update PR #46 description (endpoint, auth, agent test results)
- update wording in PR #42 (QP-2890 rewards) that says 'from the production minting catalog' to match
- Never force-push, never rebase other branches, never merge.

Both are in force. The work order above is how this run prepared the task; the request is the operator's own words, and the more current statement of intent. Where they conflict on task, constraints, or scope, the operator's request wins — say so in your report rather than choosing silently. Where the request rests on an assumption the code contradicts, follow the code and record the deviation.

Either may be empty. If both are, there is no work — say so and stop.

Whichever carries it, the work may be:

- **a plan** — a path to a plan file (read it completely) or an inline plan; execute its tasks in dependency order
- **review findings** — judge every finding, then give each one disposition in your report: **fixed**; **declined**; or **unrelated**, when it has nothing to do with this change and belongs in its own issue. A blocking finding is fixed, or declined only with the evidence that it is wrong, already satisfied, or that its smaller shape changes behavior — taste is never that evidence. A note may be declined with a one-line reason; one declined as out of scope, unrelated, or because of a boundary also goes in the discovery record below, so delivery files it. A finding with no label — a structure pass's — is declined only with evidence, like a blocking one. A defect that touches the change is fixed now, not deferred, and never declined for reaching beyond the work order's listed scope
- **a CI failure** — reproduce it, fix the cause, prove the fix
- **an existing pull request** — findings for, or a request to repair, a pull request named by number; this run must already be on its branch (see below)
- **a description** — a plain statement of what to build or change

## Reading the sources

Prose is a claim; the code is the fact. An issue body, a comment, a linked discussion, a prior report — each is somebody's belief at some past moment. Often correct, sometimes stale, never authoritative about what the code does today. Read them for intent and history, then verify anything load-bearing against the current source before acting on it. When they disagree, the code decides and you record the conflict.

Weigh by source and recency. The operator's request in this run is the most current statement of intent. A tracked item's body and its comments are older, may predate the code in front of you, and vary in how much their author verified before writing. Read them; do not inherit them. A confident claim is still a claim.

When the work or the request names a tracked item — an issue, a ticket, a document, whatever your tools can reach — read it before editing, along with the comments and linked items that can still change the outcome, its constraints, or an earlier decision. Stop following links once they no longer change what you would do.

## When the work names an existing pull request

This run must already be on that pull request's branch, or for a pull request from a fork, on the run's review branch at the pull request's head — launched onto it with `--adopt`, or from the pull request itself. Confirm that before editing with `gh pr view <number> --repo "$REPO_PATH" --json headRefName,headRefOid,isCrossRepository,maintainerCanModify`, where `REPO_PATH` is the `owner/repo` of `origin` — in a clone of a fork the CLI's default resolution targets the fork's upstream parent, and the check would read the wrong pull request. For a same-repository pull request, `git branch --show-current` must equal `headRefName`. For a fork (`isCrossRepository: true`), `git rev-parse HEAD` must equal `headRefOid` at the start of the run, and `maintainerCanModify` must be true: that flag is the author's permission for this run to push to their branch, and without it the work has nowhere to go. If either check fails, stop with `done: true, green: false` and say which check failed; never switch branches, fetch the pull request's head into this checkout, or start a replacement branch — the run's estate is fixed at launch, and work done anywhere else is invisible to it. On a match, work and commit on the current branch as usual; the pull request stays the one public surface, and later nodes push to its head and read it back by its number.

## How to work

1. Make the project runnable first: if dependencies are missing, install them with the project's own package manager in locked mode. Never update a lockfile.
2. Ground yourself before editing: read the files the work names, plus their direct callers and tests. If the repository has an `engineering.md` or a direction document (at the root or in a config directory such as `.archon/`), read them before writing code — they state the conventions and direction your change is judged against, and the values you judge review findings by. Live code beats the work item's assumptions — when they conflict, follow the code and record the deviation in your report.
3. Reproduce bugs before fixing them whenever reasonably possible; otherwise record the concrete evidence you fixed against.
4. Prefer the simplest change that solves the actual problem. If the path grows complicated, stop and reconsider the approach instead of pushing through. Existing code is evidence of what the system does, not proof that it is simple or correct: leave the path you touched simpler than you found it — split a function that outgrew itself, delete machinery your change superseded, make an implicit seam explicit. That work is cheap while you are already in the file and expensive as a separate run later, and every future reader, human or agent, pays for complexity left behind. Step 10 bounds it to the path you are already changing.
5. Write focused tests that prove the changed behavior — for a bug, a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after, when practical. No coverage theater.
6. Validate with the project's own checks: discover them from the repository itself (package scripts, task runners, CI config, contributor docs). The handoff floor is fixed: before you report done, the project's type-check, lint, and tests have all run and pass — through the project's documented aggregate command when it defines one. Narrow targeted runs are for iterating; they never substitute for the floor, and a correction round is not exempt: a fix that passes its own targeted tests but fails the project's type-check is not done. Never invent a generic command the project doesn't define; when the project defines no command for one of these classes, say so in your report instead of skipping silently.
7. Commit as you go: one commit per coherent outcome, staged by name (never `git add -A`), message written the way a human explains an outcome. No AI attribution, no generated-by footers. Never commit scratch files or anything under `/Users/raufaliyev/.archon/workspaces/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/artifacts/runs/66f348b5b2b067b15e9b65f66a26e8ab`.
8. Keep comments and documentation truthful when behavior changes.
9. Every comment must justify its existence. If a comment is needed to describe what the code does, make the code better instead — clearer names, smaller functions. Comment only what code cannot say: a non-obvious constraint, an external contract, a deliberate trade-off — written in the codebase's own idiom. Never comment to narrate a line, justify the change, or answer a reviewer; that belongs in the commit message or the report.
10. Add nothing speculative. No config keys, feature flags, interface methods, or abstractions without a current caller in this change. Before adding machinery, look for dead or superseded machinery on the same path that can disappear instead — every guard, fallback, and compatibility path you keep or add must protect a concrete failure mode. Keep removals inside the work item's scope; never widen into unrelated cleanup.
11. Enforce invariants with the project's own strongest tools. Where the project is typed, express meaningful constraints in the type system rather than in comments or runtime convention, and avoid escape hatches such as `any` or unchecked casts when a sound type is practical.
12. When the change touches agent or LLM behavior, let the model interpret and the code validate: never reconstruct intent from free prose with regexes or keyword matching — validate resolved arguments, permissions, and invariants at the tool boundary instead.

## Preserve proved unrelated work

Fix what touches the change — a defect on the path you changed, one your change makes reachable or visible, a claim your change makes false — in this change. Do not widen it into work unrelated to the change. When you prove unrelated work, judge a finding **unrelated**, or decline a note as out of scope, unrelated, or because of a boundary, preserve it without prescribing a solution: create `/Users/raufaliyev/.archon/workspaces/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/artifacts/runs/66f348b5b2b067b15e9b65f66a26e8ab/discoveries/implement.json` as a JSON array. Each record contains only `title`, `claim`, `evidence` (an array of concrete `file:line` facts or command results), `relation` (`unrelated`, `scope_conflict`, or `note` for a declined note), and `source_node` (`implement`). A scope conflict means the requested outcome, or a fix on the change, appears to require crossing a boundary the operator stated; do not cross it yourself.

Write no file when there is no proved discovery. Never add speculative filler, append to another node's file, modify a forge issue, or let an unrelated discovery change `green`. Later review owns validation and consolidation; your raw file remains evidence if that stage never runs.

## Not your job

Do not open pull requests. Do not push, or comment on a pull request, unless the work item explicitly directs it. Do not review beyond validating your own work. Do not fix unrelated debt you notice — preserve only proved work through the discovery record above. Do not merge or rebase.

## If you cannot do the work

If the work is impossible or too ambiguous to build responsibly — it names files that don't exist, a prerequisite is missing, two requirements contradict — say so plainly and stop: declare `done: true, green: false` with the blocker in `summary`, and make no speculative edits. A clear refusal is a good outcome; code built on a broken premise is not.

## Report

No one is watching this run: nothing you print survives unless it lands in this report, a commit, or a declared field, so spend no output narrating progress to a watcher who does not exist. Maintain `/Users/raufaliyev/.archon/workspaces/xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit/artifacts/runs/66f348b5b2b067b15e9b65f66a26e8ab/implementation.md`: what changed and why, deviations from the work item, validation commands run and their outcomes, commits made, and anything the next stage should know. Concise and factual — it is the durable handoff.

## Declare where things stand (every turn)

- `done` — true when another iteration would not help: the work is complete and green, or you are definitively blocked. Never with `red_cause: incomplete`: the next iteration is how the checks finish, and delivery refuses an unfinished validation
- `green` — true only when the work is complete AND every applicable project check ran this turn and passed
- `red_cause` — why the verdict is not green. When a check you ran failed: `introduced`, your change caused it; `inherited`, the same check was already failing at this run's starting commit; `environment`, the machine this run is on caused it, not any code — a database or port a parallel process holds, a missing credential, a network fault. `incomplete` when you validated the work, no check you ran failed, but not every applicable check ran — you were stopped partway (a usage limit, a killed process). A check that ran and failed takes its own cause even when others never ran. Always declared: use the empty string `""` when `green` is true, and when you are declaring a blocker on the work itself without having run checks at all
- `summary` — a few sentences: what you did, what stands, what (if anything) blocks. For `incomplete`, what stopped validation and which checks ran and passed

`inherited` and `environment` let delivery continue on red, so neither is the comfortable answer — declaring one commits you to evidence. Name the exact failing check and the concrete reason your change cannot have caused it: that check already red at the starting commit, a failure inside a subsystem your diff never touches, a resource another process holds. Put that evidence in `summary` and in your report. Without it the cause is `introduced`. Never relabel a red check to get past a gate; the pull request's real CI checks the same thing again, so a false claim buys nothing and costs a round.

Before declaring `green: true`, verify it: re-read the full diff of this run (`git status`, `git diff`, and `git log` back to the run's starting commit), confirm the work is fully covered with nothing unrelated included, confirm your report is current, and confirm the checks you cite actually ran this turn.

# User-Level Claude Instructions

These instructions apply globally across all projects and sessions.

## Planning

For config changes, integrations, and multi-step tasks: outline the plan in 3-5 bullet points and wait for approval before executing.

## Accuracy

When referencing project-specific implementations (metrics, migrations, configs), always verify claims against actual source code before stating something is 'implemented' or 'completed'. Never infer work status from metadata alone.

When asked about implementation status or what's been done, grep/read the actual source files to verify before answering. Don't infer from commit messages or ticket status alone.

1 # Authentication and environment
   2 
   3 The Quest Platform service target is `https://quests-platform.xsolla.com`.
   4 The publisher project can be a test or live project. Never change the service
   5 target or credential source as a fallback after an error.
   6 
   7 Service credentials and certificate configuration belong to the configured
   8 integration. Do not hardcode private hostnames, private CA details or service
   9 keys in this public skill. For Quest Platform publisher routes, use the
  10 versioned [API contract](qp-api-contract.md), then make a read-only request
  11 against the public gateway before any write. Production OpenAPI is
  12 intentionally unavailable; do not fetch it. Route discovery comes from the
  13 contract.
  14 
  15 ## Services
  16 
  17 The integration may expose separate services for quest configuration, event
  18 ingestion, execution read-back and Web3 catalog lookups. Use only the service
  19 that owns the requested operation. For Quest Platform configuration, event
  20 ingestion and execution read-back, use the versioned route contract above.
  21 A missing route is not replaced with a guessed path or a route from another
  22 target.
  23 
  24 ## Minting service
  25 
  26 Use the production Web3 minting service for read-only catalog validation at
  27 <!-- TODO: replace with the public hostname once the web3 team exposes one -->
  28 `https://web3-minting-service.gcp-k8s-web3-prod.srv.local`. Use only its
  29 `GET /skus` and `GET /metadata/sku/{sku}` routes, and never send the Quest
  30 Platform project API key to it. Never call a claim endpoint directly.
  31 Rewards are issued only by an activated quest.
  32 
  33 For candidate discovery, page through `GET /skus?project={project}&limit=100&offset={offset}`
  34 using the already-resolved publisher project as the lookup scope, then match
  35 the requested name against the returned item names. This project value scopes
  36 the read only; do not use it as the reward's catalog project unless the minting
  37 service returns it as `projectId`. Require HTTP 200 and a valid JSON object
  38 with a `projectId` string, numeric `count`, and `items` array on every page.
  39 Abort the lookup on any HTTP error, malformed response, or project mismatch;
  40 never treat an error as an empty page. Continue with offsets 0, 100, 200, and
  41 so on until a valid page contains no items. The optional `search` parameter
  42 reports `searchScope: "this page only"` and is not an exhaustive catalog
  43 search, so do not use it to prove uniqueness or absence. The response's
  44 `projectId` is the catalog project to carry forward. Validate each plausible
  45 candidate with `GET /metadata/sku/{sku}?project={projectId}`; require HTTP 200
  46 and a JSON `name` matching the catalog name. Abort on any failed or malformed
  47 metadata read. Read the complete catalog before deciding that a name has zero
  48 or one matches. Do not issue writes to this service.
  49 
  50 For the recipient check, read `GET /wallet/{xsolla_id}` on the same minting service.
  51 HTTP 200 with a `walletAddress` means the user has a wallet; 404 means the user has
  52 no wallet, which is a non-retryable blocker for a Web3 reward. Any other status or
  53 a malformed body aborts the check; never treat an error as a missing wallet. This is
  54 a read; do not issue writes to this service.
  55 
  56 For a named item, resolve it through the minting catalog reads above. Preserve
  57 the `projectId` returned with the verified item and validate that exact
  58 `(catalog_project, sku)` pair in the metadata read before using it in the
  59 `web3_item` body. A zero or ambiguous result stops the flow.
  60 
  61 ## Credential
  62 
  63 Use the selected merchant and project settings supplied by the configured
  64 integration. Never ask the publisher to paste a secret into chat or print a
  65 header.
  66 
  67 The shared project-local configuration uses these names. A process environment
  68 may provide the same values instead:
  69 
  70 | Value | Use |
  71 |---|---|
  72 | `XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID` | merchant scope for the project |
  73 | `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID` | Quest Platform project scope |
  74 | `XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY` | project API key |
  75 
  76 Never print, log or commit credentials or encoded headers. For Quest Platform
  77 publisher routes, the API contract requires HTTP Basic with the configured
  78 merchant ID as the username and the project API key as the password. Do not
  79 generalize this QP-specific Basic format to Catalog, Store or unrelated APIs.
  80 Do not send multiple auth schemes in one request.
  81 
  82 Read `.env` only as text; never source, execute, echo or interpolate the file.
  83 Never open `.env` in a file viewer or print it, and never paste a credential
  84 value into command text, a script file, a log or a reply. Parse the values
  85 inside the same command that sends the request, so they reach the HTTP client
  86 without ever appearing in the command line or its output. One safe pattern is a short script that parses `.env` as text and attaches
  87 `XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID` and `XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY` as the HTTP Basic pair on the
  88 request itself, so the values never reach the command line, the output or the
  89 reply. Send the request to a route from [`qp-api-contract.md`](qp-api-contract.md).
  90 Describe each call by method, route and body; do not hand the publisher a raw
  91 HTTP command.
  92 
  93 Resolve the three credential names as an all-or-nothing set:
  94 
  95 1. If all three process-environment values are present and non-empty, use that
  96    complete set.
  97 2. Otherwise, if all three project-local `.env` values are present and
  98    non-empty, use that complete set.
  99 3. Never combine process values with `.env` values. If neither source is
 100    complete, stop before network calls and tell the publisher to set
 101    `XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID`, `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID`, and
 102    `XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY` in the project-local `.env` or process environment.
 103 
 104 The project Basic credential (`XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID` plus
 105 `XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY`) is the only credential lane. Never request, print or
 106 use any other key as a fallback. If the developer asks for another lane, stop
 107 and direct them to the Quest Platform owner. Do not infer a target by probing
 108 hosts or by trying a credential against multiple gateways.
 109 
 110 The catalog project is not a credential and must come from the resolved item,
 111 never from the Quest Platform project by default.
 112 
 113 ## The merchant id in the path
 114 
 115 When the contract uses merchant and project path parameters, both must come
 116 from the same resolved credential set. Never take them from
 117 the quest body, a read-back row, an earlier answer or a guess. A developer who
 118 names another merchant or project needs the matching credential set.
 119 
 120 The server may stamp publisher and project fields from the route. Read them
 121 back after creation and stop if they do not match the resolved scope.
 122 
 123 ## Project-scoped routes
 124 
 125 Use the merchant/project-scoped Quest Platform route family in the
 126 [versioned API contract](qp-api-contract.md):
 127 
 128 | Operation | Use |
 129 |---|---|
 130 | `GET /api/v2/merchants/{merchant_id}/projects/{project_id}` | verify scope and visibility |
 131 | `GET /api/v2/merchants/{merchant_id}/projects/{project_id}/quests` | find an existing quest by paging |
 132 | `POST /api/v2/merchants/{merchant_id}/projects/{project_id}/quests` | create with `status: inactive` for a draft |
 133 | `GET` or `PUT /api/v2/merchants/{merchant_id}/projects/{project_id}/quests/{quest_id}` | read or replace one quest |
 134 
 135 Do not substitute an account-scoped, publisher-scoped or unscoped route from a
 136 different authentication lane. A route absent from the versioned contract is
 137 not called.
 138 
 139 ## When a route is missing
 140 
 141 A 404 router miss means the method and path are not deployed at that location.
 142 It is not proof of a bad credential or missing project:
 143 
 144 1. Stop and do not retry a guessed route.
 145 2. For Quest Platform routes (configuration, event ingestion, execution
 146    read-back), compare with the versioned API contract.
 147 3. If the contract documents the same operation under another route, show the
 148    developer the proposed route and ask before calling it. For a write, show
 149    the request again.
 150 4. If the operation is absent or not publisher-usable, report that it is
 151    unavailable and stop.
 152 
 153 ## Reading a 401 or 404
 154 
 155 Report the service's response body verbatim when it explains the blocker, but
 156 do not expose credential material. Keep these distinctions:
 157 
 158 - authentication required or invalid credentials means the selected
 159   credential was not accepted;
 160 - a project-not-found response is not enough to distinguish an unknown,
 161   un-onboarded or differently scoped project;
 162 - a plain router-miss response means the route is wrong or unavailable;
 163 - a missing quest response means it is not found or not visible with this
 164   credential.
 165 
 166 Do not switch to another credential, environment or route after a failure.
 167 
 168 ## Onboarding
 169 
 170 If the selected service contract documents onboarding, treat it as a separate
 171 write. Offer it only after the developer confirms that the selected project
 172 belongs to the selected merchant and provides any required non-secret names.
 173 Show the request without credentials and wait for explicit confirmation.
 174 
 175 After a timeout or server error, read the project before offering onboarding
 176 again. Never use onboarding as a probe and never infer that a 404 requires it.
 177 
 178 ## Service preflight
 179 
 180 Run one read-only preflight per service, only when the task needs that service:
 181 
 182 - Quest configuration: read the selected project and the quest list.
 183 - Event ingestion: confirm the event route and publisher Basic lane from
 184   [`qp-api-contract.md`](qp-api-contract.md) (including its production probe)
 185   before sending anything. If the contract marks the route unavailable to the
 186   publisher key, stop and report it; do not guess a host or fetch OpenAPI.
 187 - Execution read-back: confirm the read-back route, auth lane and probe from
 188   [`qp-api-contract.md`](qp-api-contract.md) before any query. If the publisher
 189   Basic lane is not accepted, or the production probe is a router miss, stop
 190   and report that read-back is unavailable; never use any other key.
 191 - Web3 catalog: resolve the named item and validate its catalog project and
 192   SKU; for a Web3 reward, when a recipient is known, also check the recipient
 193   wallet during the read-only work before the proposal, or otherwise before any
 194   publication write, and again before the event.
 195 
 196 Bring-up and preflight are GET-only. Ask before any other call.
 197 
 198 ## Scope
 199 
 200 Read the selected project and show only a short name/status summary
 201 in the normal publisher reply. Before the first write, confirm that it is the
 202 intended project. On create, verify the returned publisher and project fields.
 203 On a full `PUT`, preserve the values from the latest single-quest read.
 204 
 205 Never guess a scope or silently switch projects, merchants or credentials.
 206 
 207 ## Route families this skill does not drive
 208 
 209 Do not probe account administration, workspace administration, credential
 210 management, grant administration or data-republish routes. They are outside
 211 quest setup and require a separately documented owner-approved integration.
 212 
 213 ## Deployment status
 214 
 215 A project read does not prove that event submission, execution read-back or
 216 Web3 payout is ready. Confirm each required operation against the contract for
 217 its selected service target before using it. Never switch targets as a
 218 fallback.
 219 
 220 ## Prerequisites and lane
 221 
 222 Detail behind the skill entry point. To see which settings exist, list only the
 223 names left of `=`, for example
 224 `python3 -c 'import pathlib; print([l.split("=")[0].strip() for l in pathlib.Path(".env").read_text().splitlines() if "=" in l])'`.
 225 
 226 Follow [`auth-and-environment.md`](auth-and-environment.md) for the production credential and scope.
 227 
 228 **The configured production publisher credential is the lane**. It works only
 229 on the project-scoped routes in
 230 [`qp-api-contract.md`](qp-api-contract.md); build each
 231 route from

1 # Web3 rewards
   2 
   3 This skill supports the production Web3 reward path only. A named item always
   4 uses `web3_item` and is delivered to the player's Backpack. Do not offer
   5 `inventory_item`, Store API grants, direct Backpack grants, ERC-20 claim
   6 endpoints or a provider-default catalog as fallbacks.
   7 
   8 These are the `parameters` of a node with `type: action` and
   9 `subtype: issue_reward`:
  10 
  11 ```json
  12 {
  13   "type": "web3_item",
  14   "purpose": "quest_completion",
  15   "body": {
  16     "project": "<catalog project returned with the item>",
  17     "item_sku": "<catalog SKU>",
  18     "quantity": 1
  19   }
  20 }
  21 ```
  22 
  23 The wrapper needs a supported `type`, a non-empty `purpose` and a non-empty
  24 `body`. Use `quest_completion` for a named item unless the developer requests a
  25 different reason.
  26 
  27 ## Named item behavior
  28 
  29 When the publisher requests a named item (`<requested item>`):
  30 
  31 - resolve it only through an available supported reward capability (catalog or
  32   type-specific provider read). For production `web3_item`, the supported
  33   capability is the read-only minting catalog lookup documented in
  34   [auth and environment](auth-and-environment.md#minting-service). Page through
  35   the catalog, match the requested name, and validate candidate metadata before
  36   using it. Never use public web search for catalog lookup;
  37 - when the capability is available and returns exactly one verified candidate,
  38   use that candidate's catalog project and SKU in the `web3_item` body;
  39 - when it returns multiple plausible candidates, ask the publisher to choose
  40   before any Quest Platform write;
  41 - if the service is unavailable or rejects the read, stop before any Quest
  42   Platform write and report that the item lookup service could not be reached;
  43   do not say the publisher's catalog needs connecting. If a completed search
  44   returns zero candidates, say the item was not found and suggest checking its
  45   exact name or whether it is enabled. Do not ask the publisher to type a
  46   catalog project or SKU: a typed value is not a verified candidate;
  47 - default quantity to one and show it in the concise proposal;
  48 - never guess an SKU or silently substitute another reward type
  49   (`inventory_item`, Store API grants, direct Backpack grants, ERC-20 claim
  50   endpoints, or a provider-default catalog).
  51 
  52 Never ask whether the destination is Backpack. Preserve the catalog project
  53 returned by the verified candidate; never copy the Quest Platform project as
  54 the catalog project by default.
  55 
  56 ## `web3_item`
  57 
  58 An NFT from the production minting catalog:
  59 
  60 ```json
  61 {
  62   "type": "web3_item",
  63   "purpose": "quest_completion",
  64   "body": {
  65     "project": "<catalog project>",
  66     "item_sku": "<string or array>",
  67     "quantity": 1
  68   }
  69 }
  70 ```
  71 
  72 `quantity` must be a non-negative integer. For a named item, use a real SKU
  73 returned by the catalog lookup. Omitting `item_sku` lets the provider choose an
  74 item and is not allowed for a named reward.
  75 
  76 The production runtime must enforce the once-per-user-per-quest rule. When a
  77 confirmed payout already exists for the same user and quest, a repeat event
  78 must not mint a second item. If the earlier payout is unresolved, stop and
  79 escalate rather than resend the event.
  80 
  81 ## `web3_token`
  82 
  83 Production runs have ERC-20 payouts disabled. A production quest with a
  84 `web3_token` action fails at payout. When a production request asks for a
  85 token payout, stop before any Quest Platform write, say that token payouts are
  86 not available for the project yet, and offer a named item reward instead. Do not ask the publisher for a token
  87 binding or decimals, because no production binding can make the payout work.
  88 Use the shape below only when the Quest Platform owner has confirmed that
  89 ERC-20 payouts are enabled for the project.
  90 
  91 An ERC-20 payout, only when the token binding and runtime contract are
  92 confirmed:
  93 
  94 ```json
  95 {
  96   "type": "web3_token",
  97   "purpose": "quest_completion",
  98   "body": {
  99     "project": "<token project>",
 100     "item_sku": "<bound token SKU>",
 101     "amount": 10000
 102   }
 103 }
 104 ```
 105 
 106 `amount` must be a positive integer in the token's base units and within the
 107 selected target's contract limit. Confirm the token decimals and binding with
 108 the owner of that target. Never guess them.
 109 
 110 `web3_item.body.project` selects the catalog only when the deployed reward
 111 worker supports it. A worker without that support ignores the field and mints
 112 against its configured default project, so the item can reach the wallet but
 113 show without the catalog name. When a read-back shows a project different from
 114 `body.project`, report a delivery mismatch, not a success, and do not send the
 115 event again.
 116 
 117 ## Recipient
 118 
 119 Both Web3 reward types need an `xsolla_id` in the event and a production wallet
 120 for that user. When a recipient is known, check the wallet with the recipient read in
 121 [`auth-and-environment.md`](auth-and-environment.md#minting-service) during the
 122 read-only work before the proposal, or otherwise before any publication write.
 123 Check it again before the event. A missing wallet is a non-retryable blocker,
 124 not an approval step. Confirm the wallet source is the Backpack-compatible
 125 managed wallet required by the production integration.
 126 
 127 ## Payout exposure in the proposal
 128 
 129 Show three bounds in the publication proposal:
 130 
 131 - **Per event and user:** `web3_item` is `quantity × selected SKU count`;
 132   for a once-per-user named item at quantity one this is one NFT.
 133   `web3_token` is `amount`.
 134 - **Per user for the quest:** apply the effective activation limit to the
 135   per-event quantity. For a confirmed once-per-user named item this is one NFT
 136   per user and quest; for quantity greater than one or multiple SKUs, multiply
 137   by `quantity × selected SKU count`. For `web3_token`, multiply `amount` by
 138   the maximum qualifying events for that user.
 139 - **Total quest exposure:** multiply the per-user bound by the maximum number
 140   of eligible users. If the user population, event count, activation limit or
 141   date window is not finite, report the total as **unbounded**.
 142 
 143 Do not publish a repeatable Web3 reward without showing these calculations in
 144 the proposal. An unbounded total needs an explicit acknowledgement in that
 145 same approval.
 146 
 147 ## Completion evidence
 148 
 149 An execution marked `COMPLETED` proves only that the reward action completed
 150 according to the production execution contract. It does not by itself prove a
 151 Backpack display, wallet balance or on-chain finality. Report only the evidence
 152 returned by the production read-back and never resend an event after an

  17     "item_sku": "<catalog SKU>",
  18     "quantity": 1
  19   }
  20 }
  21 ```

  27 ## Named item behavior
  28 
  29 When the publisher requests a named item (`<requested item>`):
  30 
  31 - resolve it only through an available supported reward capability (catalog or
  32   type-specific provider read). For production `web3_item`, the supported
  33   capability is the read-only minting catalog lookup documented in
  34   [auth and environment](auth-and-environment.md#minting-service). Page through
  35   the catalog, match the requested name, and validate candidate metadata before
  36   using it. Never use public web search for catalog lookup;
  37 - when the capability is available and returns exactly one verified candidate,
  38   use that candidate's catalog project and SKU in the `web3_item` body;
  39 - when it returns multiple plausible candidates, ask the publisher to choose
  40   before any Quest Platform write;
  41 - if the service is unavailable or rejects the read, stop before any Quest
  42   Platform write and report that the item lookup service could not be reached;
  43   do not say the publisher's catalog needs connecting. If a completed search
  44   returns zero candidates, say the item was not found and suggest checking its
  45   exact name or whether it is enabled. Do not ask the publisher to type a
  46   catalog project or SKU: a typed value is not a verified candidate;
  47 - default quantity to one and show it in the concise proposal;
  48 - never guess an SKU or silently substitute another reward type
  49   (`inventory_item`, Store API grants, direct Backpack grants, ERC-20 claim
  50   endpoints, or a provider-default catalog).
  51 
  52 Never ask whether the destination is Backpack. Preserve the catalog project
  53 returned by the verified candidate; never copy the Quest Platform project as
  54 the catalog project by default.

  56 ## `web3_item`
  57 
  58 An NFT from the production minting catalog:
  59 
  60 ```json
  61 {
  62   "type": "web3_item",
  63   "purpose": "quest_completion",
  64   "body": {
  65     "project": "<catalog project>",
  66     "item_sku": "<string or array>",
  67     "quantity": 1
  68   }
  69 }
  70 ```
  71 
  72 `quantity` must be a non-negative integer. For a named item, use a real SKU
  73 returned by the catalog lookup. Omitting `item_sku` lets the provider choose an
  74 item and is not allowed for a named reward.
  75 
  76 The production runtime must enforce the once-per-user-per-quest rule. When a
  77 confirmed payout already exists for the same user and quest, a repeat event
  78 must not mint a second item. If the earlier payout is unresolved, stop and
  79 escalate rather than resend the event.
  80 
  81 ## `web3_token`
  82 
  83 Production runs have ERC-20 payouts disabled. A production quest with a
  84 `web3_token` action fails at payout. When a production request asks for a
  85 token payout, stop before any Quest Platform write, say that token payouts are
  86 not available for the project yet, and offer a named item reward instead. Do not ask the publisher for a token
  87 binding or decimals, because no production binding can make the payout work.
  88 Use the shape below only when the Quest Platform owner has confirmed that
  89 ERC-20 payouts are enabled for the project.
  90 
  91 An ERC-20 payout, only when the token binding and runtime contract are
  92 confirmed:
  93 
  94 ```json
  95 {
  96   "type": "web3_token",
  97   "purpose": "quest_completion",
  98   "body": {
  99     "project": "<token project>",
 100     "item_sku": "<bound token SKU>",
 101     "amount": 10000
 102   }
 103 }
 104 ```
 105 
 106 `amount` must be a positive integer in the token's base units and within the
 107 selected target's contract limit. Confirm the token decimals and binding with
 108 the owner of that target. Never guess them.
 109 
 110 `web3_item.body.project` selects the catalog only when the deployed reward
 111 worker supports it. A worker without that support ignores the field and mints
 112 against its configured default project, so the item can reach the wallet but
 113 show without the catalog name. When a read-back shows a project different from
 114 `body.project`, report a delivery mismatch, not a success, and do not send the
 115 event again.
 116 
 117 ## Recipient
 118 
 119 Both Web3 reward types need an `xsolla_id` in the event and a production wallet
 120 for that user. When a recipient is known, check the wallet with the recipient read in
 121 [`auth-and-environment.md`](auth-and-environment.md#minting-service) during the
 122 read-only work before the proposal, or otherwise before any publication write.
 123 Check it again before the event. A missing wallet is a non-retryable blocker,
 124 not an approval step. Confirm the wallet source is the Backpack-compatible
 125 managed wallet required by the production integration.
 126 
 127 ## Payout exposure in the proposal
 128 
 129 Show three bounds in the publication proposal:
 130 
 131 - **Per event and user:** `web3_item` is `quantity × selected SKU count`;
 132   for a once-per-user named item at quantity one this is one NFT.
 133   `web3_token` is `amount`.
 134 - **Per user for the quest:** apply the effective activation limit to the
 135   per-event quantity. For a confirmed once-per-user named item this is one NFT
 136   per user and quest; for quantity greater than one or multiple SKUs, multiply
 137   by `quantity × selected SKU count`. For `web3_token`, multiply `amount` by
 138   the maximum qualifying events for that user.
 139 - **Total quest exposure:** multiply the per-user bound by the maximum number
 140   of eligible users. If the user population, event count, activation limit or
 141   date window is not finite, report the total as **unbounded**.
 142 
 143 Do not publish a repeatable Web3 reward without showing these calculations in

 149 An execution marked `COMPLETED` proves only that the reward action completed

 152 returned by the production read-back and never resend an event after an
 153 uncertain result.

 148    requests follow [Choosing a trigger](references/node-subtypes.md#choosing-a-trigger).
 149 4. **Edit.** Read, change, full `PUT` per
 150    [Editing](references/quest-document.md#editing). Warn that `PUT` replaces the
 151    whole document and an active quest's edit goes live. Show a before/after
 152    diff, get approval, read back, and pause per
 153    [Pausing](references/quest-document.md#pausing).
 154 5. **Event.** Allowed only after the gate in
 155    [`events.md`](references/events.md) passes, with its own approval and exact
 156    payload. Until then do not send an event; say event execution is not yet
 157    verified. If the contract marks the route unavailable to the publisher key,
 158    report that blocker at this step. Never resend after an uncertain response. Details:
 159    [Flow step detail](references/events.md#flow-step-detail-submitting-an-event).
 160 6. **Verify.** Follow [`verification.md`](references/verification.md): correlate
 161    the event, report whether the quest ran and which action nodes completed.
 162    Details: [Flow step detail](references/verification.md#flow-step-detail-verifying).
 163 7. **Delete.** Only quests the developer names, one per call, after a fresh read
 164    and an explicit yes. `DELETE` is a soft delete with no restore route; see
 165    [Deleting](references/quest-document.md#deleting).
 166

 168 
 169 Full text: [writes and credentials](references/auth-and-environment.md#safety-stops-for-writes-and-credentials),
 170 [proposals and actions](references/quest-document.md#safety-stops-for-proposals-and-actions),
 171 [events and failed rewards](references/events.md#safety-stops-for-events-and-failed-rewards),
 172 [execution reads](references/verification.md#scope-of-execution-reads).
 173 
 174 - Show the resolved scope before the first write; ask separately before any
 175   other non-GET call, showing the exact body first.
 176 - Each event needs its own payload and yes. After a timeout or `FAILED` reward
 177   action, do not resend.
 178 - Never point `send_http_webhook` at a private service or an unapproved host.
 179 - Read executions only by the developer's own quest id after confirming
 180   ownership; never use an internal key.
 181 - Branch errors on HTTP status per
 182   [Errors](references/auth-and-environment.md#errors). `ID 0` is a valid
 183   merchant and project ID; never treat it as absent.

### send_http_webhook

```json
{"url": "<developer-supplied HTTP or HTTPS URL>"}
```

`url` is the only modeled parameter. It must be a non-empty HTTP or HTTPS URL
with a host. The runtime sends the event by HTTP POST as JSON, including user
identifiers. Never treat an arbitrary URL as a harmless placeholder.

- **Approved** means an endpoint the developer owns or controls and names
  explicitly. A public request bin receives the event too; use one only after
  the developer acknowledges it while building the publication proposal (not as
  a separate post-approval gate).
- Never point it at a private platform service or the minting service. A
  webhook cannot pay out and must never carry credentials. To pay out, use an
  `issue_reward` Web3 reward with the values listed in `rewards.md`.
- A reserved host such as `https://e2e-sink.invalid/hook` is never written and
  must never appear in a publication proposal. Replace it with the developer's
  approved endpoint before showing the proposal.
- The webhook fires only after the quest is active. State that timing and the
  destination in the publication proposal so the one approval covers it. Do not
  ask again before activation unless the endpoint changed after approval, in
  which case show the revised proposal and request approval again.

An error response, timeout or unresolvable host fails the action. The runtime
may retry it, so the endpoint may receive the same event more than once.
Tell the developer to deduplicate by `idempotency_key`.

### send_xsolla_app_notification

```json
{
  "topic": "<developer-supplied topic>",
  "notification_type": "<developer-supplied notification type>",
  "title": "<developer-supplied title>",
  "message": "<developer-supplied message>",
  "data": {}
}
```

| `idempotency_key` | yes | valid, non-zero UUID; generate a fresh one per event |
| `name` | yes | must match the quest trigger's `event_name` |
| `client_timestamp` | yes | RFC3339 |
| `user_ids` | yes | at least one entry |
| `quest_id` | no | valid UUID when present; restricts matching to one quest |
| `scope` | no | default `private` unless the developer asks otherwise |
| `publisher` | yes for Basic lane | must match the quest's read-back scope; positive integer Xsolla IDs |
| `properties` | no | use only values accepted by the contract; never include secrets |

`user_ids[].identifier_type` is `xsolla_id`, `gamer_id`, `guest_id` or `email`
per the contract. A Web3 reward requires an `xsolla_id` whose user already has
a wallet. Check it with the recipient read in [`auth-and-environment.md`](auth-and-environment.md#minting-service) before submitting.

A successful response returns `event_id` (and echoes `idempotency_key`). Keep
`event_id` and use it to correlate the read-only execution result when
read-back is publisher-usable. If the response shape differs, follow the
versioned contract, not a guessed OpenAPI fetch.

jobs:
  sync:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Don't re-trigger on this workflow's own commit.
    if: github.actor != 'github-actions[bot]'
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

      - name: Sync skills and CLAUDE.md
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          rm -rf .cursor/skills
          mkdir -p .cursor/skills
          for skill_dir in skills/*/; do
            skill_name=$(basename "$skill_dir")
            if [ -f "${skill_dir}SKILL.md" ]; then
              cp -R "$skill_dir" ".cursor/skills/${skill_name}"
              echo "Synced: .cursor/skills/${skill_name}"
            fi
          done

          cp AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
          echo "Synced: CLAUDE.md"

      - name: Commit generated files
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add .cursor/skills/ CLAUDE.md
          if git diff --staged --quiet; then
            echo "Already in sync — nothing to commit."
            exit 0
          fi

- Re-list or `GET` right before deleting, and show each quest's name, id,

- Delete one quest per call. Stop on the first non-200 and report it; after a
  timeout or 5xx, `GET` the quest to check before trying again.
- Re-list afterwards and show that the deleted quests are gone.

## Conversation contract

Keep the publisher experience business-first and progressive:

- Finish all read-only bring-up before any proposal: project GET, reward
  resolution through an available supported capability (see
  [`rewards.md`](rewards.md)), the player action,
  complete graph, proposed schedule and repeat limits. Do not seek plan
  approval before those GETs.
- Show one concise proposal: publisher project name; what the player does; the
  selected reward in business terms; quantity or amount; schedule; repeat limit
  and payout impact. Omit service names, routes, auth, implementation fields
  and narration. Ask only for approval of this draft quest. If the publisher
  wants a change, they will say so; do not request separate confirmation of
  the schedule or event name.
- Propose safe defaults instead of asking for implementation fields. For a
  gameplay quest, use `liveops` internally but describe it as a gameplay quest.
  Do not show `type` in the proposal. For an item reward, propose quantity one,
  purpose `quest_completion`, and one payout per player. Use `AI Toolkit` as
  the internal creator label unless another name was supplied. For a new quest,
  use the publisher's start or start at activation. Use the publisher's end,
  otherwise add their requested duration to the start, otherwise add 7 days.
  Do not ask for missing dates.
- For a named item (`<requested item>`), resolve via
  [`rewards.md`](rewards.md). Never guess an SKU,
  substitute a reward type, or use public web search for catalog lookup. Stop
  before any Quest Platform write when the resolver is absent, unavailable, or
  returns zero candidates; ask the publisher to choose when multiple candidates
  are plausible. The optional headless Web Shop module is independent of the
  quest flow; follow
  `web-shop-module.md` only when
  explicitly requested.
- Use the event name the publisher supplied, or derive a stable `snake_case`
  name from the stated player action (for example, `monster_defeated`). Show
  that name in the draft without asking the publisher to confirm it or flagging
  it as an open question. If the publisher names a different game event later,
  revise the draft then.
- One approval of the exact proposal authorizes create, configure, activate and
  read-back. Test events and shop source edits need separate consent. The
  approval request names only publication; never offer, promise or bundle a
  test event in it. Offer the event after publication, with its payload. If an
  answer requests a material change after approval, show the revised draft
  and ask for approval of that change before writing it.
- A Web Shop quest section is optional and requires an explicit request. For
  an existing headless shop, an explicit request to add or update it authorizes
  those source edits; quest publication approval alone does not. For a new shop,
  ask whether to opt in. Keep the module inside catalog content, never in
  navigation, and follow `web-shop-module.md`.
  Resolve the public URL from the known production host and the connected
  project scope; never ask the developer to supply it or gate integration on a
  live endpoint readiness check.
- Keep merchant IDs, project IDs, auth lanes, headers, hostnames, service names,
  internal paths and workflow narration out of normal replies. Never reveal
  credentials. Use **Summary**, **Proposed setup**, **Need from you**,
  **Next step** when practical; omit empty sections.

## Safety stops for proposals and actions

- **Show the proposed defaults in the draft.** Use the defaults in the
  Conversation contract when the intent is clear and ask only for approval of
  the complete draft. For a gameplay item quest, the trigger, `issue_reward`
  action, quantity one,
  `quest_completion` purpose and one payout per player may be proposed
  together. Never silently choose between multiple catalog matches or
  materially different reward effects; those are blockers to a complete draft.
  A write's yes counts only for the exact draft shown. If the publisher requests
  a change, show the revised draft and ask for approval of it. Keep separate
  approvals for later edits that change live behavior and for each event. For
  "start now", approval covers activation time in UTC and the stated duration;
  do not request a new approval because the clock advanced.
- No action is side-effect free by default. For a smoke test, offer the no-op
  in [`node-subtypes.md`](node-subtypes.md) rather than a
  real reward (placeholders `e2e-noop`, `e2e-sink.invalid`). For publication
  or a smoke test, say production events are not verified until the events
  preflight passes ([production event gate](events.md#production-event-gate)).
- When an external action is part of the proposal, say what it will do once
  active. The publication approval covers that impact for the approved quest.
  An `issue_reward` can create real payouts; `send_http_webhook` sends event
  data to an external URL; `send_xsolla_app_notification` sends a user
  notification. Activate a `webshop_personalization` node only after the
  developer acknowledges that it is a no-op. For an active quest whose only
  action it is, say before any edit or event that it does nothing and a
  `COMPLETED` row proves only that the quest ran; a `PUT` that keeps it active
  needs that acknowledgement, a pause does not.
- Never point `send_http_webhook` at a private service or an
  [unapproved host](node-subtypes.md#send_http_webhook): a webhook
  cannot mint. To pay out a named item, use an `issue_reward` Web3 reward with
  the verified candidate's catalog project and SKU.
- For a named item reward, propose an explicit `per_user` limit of one and
  explain it as one `<requested item>` per player. Do not ask about Backpack or
  regular versus Web3 delivery. Ask only if the developer asks for repeatable
  or unlimited rewards, or if the intended repeat behavior is otherwise
  ambiguous. For other rewards with no `activation_limits`, show unlimited
  repeat in the publication proposal; the one approval covers it. Do not
  silently choose unlimited behavior.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("skills/quest-setup/references/auth-and-environment.md")
t = p.read_text()
start = t.index("## Minting service\n"); end = t.index("## Credential\n")
new = '''## Store admin catalog

Resolve a named `web3_item` through the Store admin virtual items reads at
`https://store.xsolla.com/api/v2/project/{project_id}/admin/items/virtual_items`,
with `{project_id}` set to the resolved `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID`. Use only these
two GET routes:

| Route | Use |
|---|---|
| `GET .../admin/items/virtual_items?limit=50&offset={offset}` | page the full catalog |
| `GET .../admin/items/virtual_items/sku/{sku}` | validate one chosen SKU |

Never issue a `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` to any Store admin route, even
when the publisher asks for it; creating or editing items is outside this
skill. Never call a claim endpoint directly. Rewards are issued only by an
activated quest.

Page with offsets 0, 50, 100 and so on while the page's `has_more` is `true`.
Require HTTP 200 and a JSON object with an `items` array, a boolean `has_more`
and a numeric `total_items_count` on every page. Abort the lookup on a 401, any
other non-200 status, a malformed body, or a final item count different from
`total_items_count`; never treat an aborted read as an empty catalog. Read the

5. **No IDs or hosts in replies.** Outside the event
   payload, never show merchant, project or player IDs, hosts, service names
   or environment names to the publisher (a reward item's SKU and image URL
   are fine). Every reply starts with a `##`
   heading: no lead-in line such as "Perfect!" or a recap before it.
6. **Never claim delivery.** Report what the read-backs show, nothing more.
## Store admin catalog

Resolve a named `web3_item` through the Store admin virtual items reads at
`https://store.xsolla.com/api/v2/project/{project_id}/admin/items/virtual_items`,
with `{project_id}` set to the resolved `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID`. Use only these
two GET routes:

| Route | Use |
|---|---|
| `GET .../admin/items/virtual_items?limit=50&offset={offset}` | page the full catalog |
| `GET .../admin/items/virtual_items/sku/{sku}` | validate one chosen SKU |

Never issue a `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` to any Store admin route, even
when the publisher asks for it; creating or editing items is outside this
skill. Never call a claim endpoint directly. Rewards are issued only by an
activated quest.

Page with offsets 0, 50, 100 and so on while the page's `has_more` is `true`.
Require HTTP 200 and a JSON object with an `items` array, a boolean `has_more`
and a numeric `total_items_count` on every page. Abort the lookup on a 401, any
other non-200 status, a malformed body, or a final item count different from
`total_items_count`; never treat an aborted read as an empty catalog. Read the
complete catalog before deciding that a name has zero, one or several matches.

Each item has `sku`, a localized `name` object (for example `{"en": "Fire
Sword"}`), a localized `description` or `null`, `image_url` or `null`, `type`,
`is_enabled`, `is_show_in_store`, `periods`, `groups` and `attributes`. Match
the requested name case-insensitively against `name.en` first, then against the
other locales. An exact match is a candidate; when there is no exact match,
items whose name contains the requested words are candidates to show, never to
pick on your own.

Only an item that is mintable is a valid `web3_item` SKU: `is_enabled` and
`is_show_in_store` are both `true`, and `periods` is empty or one period
contains the current time. When the requested name matches only items that
fail this rule, say the item exists but is not available as a Web3 reward
(disabled, hidden from the store or outside its sale period) and stop.

Validate the chosen SKU, including one the publisher typed, with the single-item
read. Require HTTP 200, the same `sku` and name, and the mintable rule above.
A 404 means the SKU is not in the catalog. Abort on any other failure. The
catalog project for the `web3_item` body is the `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID` both reads
were scoped to. A zero or ambiguous result stops the flow.

Observed 2026-10-05 on the kit's production project (49 virtual items):

- HTTP Basic with `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID` (documented `basicAuth`) and with
  `XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID` (`basicMerchantAuth`) as the username both return 200.
  No header or a wrong key returns 401 with `errorCode` 1501. Use
  `XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID`.
- `limit` below 1 returns 422. Values up to 10001 returned 200; the whole
  catalog fit on one page at every limit, so no server cap was observed. Page
  by `has_more`, not by item count.
- The single-item read returns the same item object; an unknown SKU returns
  404 with `errorCode` 4001.
- Parity: the minting service's SKU list held 47 SKUs, all in the admin list
  and identical to the public client catalog. The two admin-only items were
  one with `is_show_in_store: false` and one whose only period starts in the
  future. `type`, `groups` and `attributes` did not separate them.

## Recipient wallet

The recipient check is the only call to the Web3 minting service:
`GET https://web3-minting-service.gcp-k8s-web3-prod.srv.local/wallet/{xsolla_id}`.
It resolves only on the corporate network and needs no credential; never send
the project API key to it and never issue writes to it.

HTTP 200 with a `walletAddress` means the user has a wallet; 404 means the user
has no wallet, which is a non-retryable blocker for a Web3 reward. Any other
status or a malformed body aborts the check; never treat an error as a missing
wallet. When the host cannot be resolved or reached, report the wallet check as
not run, never as "no wallet" and never as a confirmed wallet. Name the
unverified recipient wallet in the proposal or the event payload review so the
publisher's approval covers it.

## Credential
